title: Metta's far enemy
hook: ill will is metta's opposite; kindness dissolves it slowly

segments.voice: Yesterday, metta, revisited, and your line: kindness, not clinging. Did you find a string on one of your kindnesses? Day two hundred thirty-four.

The coworker who chews loudly. The neighbor who parks across your driveway. The relative who always makes that one comment at dinner. Ill will rarely starts big. It starts as an irritation, and then it gets fed: replayed in the shower, told to a friend, rehearsed in imaginary arguments where you always win. After a while, just seeing the person's name can tighten a jaw. Yesterday we met metta's near enemy, the one that looks like kindness. Today, the one that looks nothing like it. Today: metta's far enemy.
screen: `THE LOUD CHEWER, THE DRIVEWAY.` → `IRRITATION, FED AND REPLAYED.` → `THE JAW TIGHTENS.`

segments.voice: The Visuddhimagga names metta's far enemy plainly: ill will, the Pali vyapada, the wish for someone to suffer. It's called far because it's the opposite of kindness, and easy to recognize. The danger isn't that you'll mistake it. The danger is that it's comfortable, and it grows. So the manual gives a whole toolkit for softening it, one method after another, for when the first doesn't work. One tool: look at what anger does to the one who holds it. The manual compares it to picking up a burning coal to throw at someone: your own hand gets burned first. Another: look for one good quality in the person, even a small one. If their actions are rough, maybe their speech is kind; if not that, maybe their heart has something good in it. The manual compares this to a traveler, hot and thirsty, who finds a pond covered in moss, sweeps the moss aside with his hands, and drinks. Another: remember that everyone is the owner of their own actions: your anger won't fix theirs. One more is disarmingly simple: give the person a gift. The manual says a gift can soften a long-held grudge in a moment. And one of the strangest: take the person apart, in your mind, into hair, skin, bones, warmth and breath, and ask, which part am I angry at? It's hard to stay angry at an elbow. None of this is quick. Kindness dissolves ill will slowly, the way water wears down stone. You met the root of this in the Dhammapada's fifth verse: hatred never ends by hatred. Here is the practical how.
screen: `VYAPADA — ILL WILL.` · `THE BURNING COAL.` · `SWEEP THE MOSS AND DRINK.` · `A GIFT, AND WHICH PART AM I ANGRY AT?` · then, large: `ILL WILL SOFTENS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one small irritation, one person who annoys you a little. Keep it small. Notice where the irritation lives in your body. Now try one tool from the manual. Look for one good quality in them, however small: they love their dog, they're kind to the cashier, they work hard. Sweep the moss aside and find it. Then, if you can, offer them one breath of the old wish: may you be well. Notice any softening, even a little. The bell holds the time.
Byāpāda. Ill will, the plain opposite of kindness: the manual's tools soften it slowly, one method at a time.
Your line: ill will softens. Today, when that one irritation shows up, sweep the moss aside and find one good thing in the person. Day two hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers draw on the Visuddhimagga's methods for softening resentment, such as recalling a person's good qualities or giving a gift, and practitioners send metta to difficult people in small, gradual steps.

match.prompt: match each tool in the manual's toolkit.
pairs: anger burns your own hand first
sweep aside, find the good, drink
which part am I angry at?

fork.setup: you've tried wishing a difficult neighbor well, and the resentment won't budge. what does the manual suggest?
options: give up on metta for them.
try another method: find one good quality, or give a small gift.
wait for them to apologize first.
fork.reveal: the Visuddhimagga offers method after method for when the first doesn't work, including recalling a good quality and giving a gift.

original.note: Pali byāpāda (also vyāpāda): ill will, metta's far enemy.

trapdoor: what you thought: the opposite of kindness is just not being nice.
what it means: ill will, the wish for someone to suffer, softened slowly by kindness and the manual's tools.
what a scholar hears: Visuddhimagga IX lists a sequence of methods for removing resentment (patigha), from reviewing its dangers to the gift and the 'resolution into elements'.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga IX (removing resentment: the burning coal, the mossy pond, giving a gift, resolution into elements)

notes: Visuddhimagga IX paraphrased: burning coal / firebrand simile, the moss-covered pond simile, ownership of kamma, giving a gift, resolution into elements. Confirm each simile's wording and order (approx. IX.15–39).
The Pali for ill will is given as byapada/vyapada; confirm the Devanagari spelling ब्यापाद (the variant व्यापाद is also found).
'The way water wears down stone' is the writer's image, not the manual's.
